episodes.name: 2013: taper tantrum and the FCNR(B) swap window

facts.text: The RBI announced a special window on 4 September 2013 to swap fresh FCNR(B) dollar deposits of at least three years’ maturity at a fixed 3.5% a year, open until 30 November; banks’ overseas borrowing limit was raised from 50% to 100% of tier-I capital, swappable at 100bp below the market rate.
The rupee had fallen about 30% against the dollar between April and August 2013.
The two swap windows mobilised about $34 billion, according to the RBI; about $26–27 billion of it came through FCNR(B) deposits and about $8 billion through banks’ overseas borrowing.
The deposits matured mostly in 2016: FCNR(B) deposits fell from $44.11 billion at end-September 2016 to $20.85 billion at end-December 2016.

episodes.name: 2026: the oil shock and the second FCNR(B) window

facts.text: The RBI announced a concessional US dollar–rupee swap facility on 5 June 2026, operational from 8 June, for fresh FCNR(B) deposits of three to five years, external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowings.
On 14 August the RBI brought the FCNR(B) deadline forward from 30 September to 31 August; the ECB and overseas borrowing windows stay open until 31 December 2026.

RBI provisional figures of 2 September: $127.23 billion of FCNR(B) deposits by 31 August, and $136.38 billion including ECBs ($3.89 billion) and overseas borrowing ($5.26 billion). Later RBI data (21 September) put FCNR(B) mobilisation at $132.98 billion.
facts.source: Policy Circle; Investmates, citing RBI releases

facts.text: That is roughly four times the 2013 window, with a much smaller interest-rate gap: the India–US five-year yield spread was about 720bp on 4 September 2013 and about 210bp on 4 August 2026.
